**The Edges of the Map**

For most of human history, maps had edges. Not just the physical edges of the parchment, but epistemic ones: places where knowledge simply ran out, and the cartographer, facing a blank, had to decide what to do with it. The famous solutions were sea serpents, whirlpools swallowing ships, warnings in Latin. *Terra incognita*. *Hic sunt dracones*. Here be dragons. The exact phrase survives on only one artifact, the Hunt-Lenox Globe from around 1510, but the sentiment was everywhere. Beyond this line, the map admitted, we are guessing, and our guesses are frightened.

What moves me about those old maps is not the monsters but the honesty. A blank space confessed something. The cartographer declared, in public, that the world was bigger than his knowledge of it. Modern maps make no such confession. They are seamless, satellite-fed, total. You can zoom into a street corner in a city you will never visit and read the names of its coffee shops. The feeling this produces is that the world is finished, that exploration is a hobby for historians. But this is an illusion, and the easiest way to see through it is to go down.

The ocean covers about seventy percent of the planet, and we have mapped most of it the way you might map a house by flying over it in a plane. We know the broad shape; we do not know the details. By some measures we have better topographic data for Mars than for our own seafloor, because Mars has no water in the way. Roughly a quarter of the ocean bottom has been mapped at high resolution. The rest is a suggestion. In the entire twentieth century, fewer people reached the bottom of the Mariana Trench than walked on the Moon, even though the trench is only eleven kilometers straight down, a distance you could drive in seven minutes on a highway, except that no highway, no sunlight, and almost nothing human has ever gone there.

Consider the eel. For most of recorded history, nobody could find eel eggs, eel young, or eel reproductive organs, anywhere. Aristotle concluded that eels emerged spontaneously from mud. Pliny thought they rubbed themselves against rocks and the scrapings came alive. As a young man in Trieste, Sigmund Freud spent a summer dissecting hundreds of eels in search of testes and failed, which is one of the great footnotes in the history of science. It turned out that European eels mature sexually only during a vast migration across the Atlantic to the Sargasso Sea, a hypothesis the Danish oceanographer Johannes Schmidt assembled after two decades of chasing ever-smaller larvae across the ocean, and one only confirmed by tracking tagged adults within the last few years. No human being has ever watched an eel spawn. We have sequenced genomes and landed robots on comets, and we still cannot tell you exactly what one of the world's most common fish does at the most important moment of its life.

I love the eel story because it corrects a certain chronological arrogance. We assume the blank spaces on the map were filled in by our grandparents, that the remaining mysteries live only at the exotic frontiers: dark matter, the origin of life, the first fraction of a second after the Big Bang. But the unknown is not exotic. It is local, patient, and often wet. Nobody knows, in any settled and unified way, why we sleep. We have good theories (memory consolidation, cellular cleanup, the nightly pruning of synapses) and we have the brute fact that essentially every animal with a brain does it, at the cost of lying defenseless for hours, which means evolution insists on it while we still cannot fully say why. You will spend a third of your life doing something science cannot entirely explain. The dragons are in the bedroom.

And then there is the most familiar blank space of all: other people. I have never once experienced your experience. I infer it, model it, guess at it from your face and your words, and the guessing works well enough that we build whole civilizations on top of it, but it remains guessing. Every person you pass on the street is an unmapped interior continent. Even the people you love best are partly legend, partly report, partly your own cartography projected onto them. This can sound lonely, and sometimes it is, but I think it is also the source of everything decent in us. Curiosity about another mind is just respect wearing its work clothes. Love, at least one kind of love, is the decision to keep exploring a coast you will never finish charting.

There is an old saying that as the island of knowledge grows, so does the shoreline of wonder. I used to find this discouraging. If every answer births two new questions, then inquiry is a treadmill and ignorance is infinite either way. But I have come to think the metaphor is the best news available. A finite island in an infinite sea means there is no finish line at which curiosity becomes obsolete, no moment when the species closes its notebooks and says *done*. The map will always have edges, because having edges is what a map is. Total knowledge would not be a completed map; it would be the end of mapmaking, which is to say the end of everything interesting.

So I have made my peace with the blank spaces. More than peace, really. I have started to think of them as the point. The cartographers of six centuries ago wrote their fear into the margins in the form of dragons, and fear was the wrong emotion, but the impulse was right. Something is out there, past the edge of what we know. It has always been out there. The correct caption for the blank was never a warning. It was an invitation.

**The Edges of the Map**

For most of human history, maps had edges. Not just the physical edges of the parchment, but epistemic ones: places where knowledge simply ran out, and the cartographer, facing a blank, had to decide what to do with it. The famous solutions were sea serpents, whirlpools swallowing ships, warnings in Latin. Hic sunt dracones. Here be dragons. The phrase survives on exactly one artifact, the Hunt-Lenox Globe from around 1510, but the sentiment was everywhere. Beyond this line, the map said, we are guessing, and our guesses are frightened.

[~105 words]

What moves me about those old maps is not the monsters but the honesty. A blank space admitted something. The cartographer confessed, in public, that the world was bigger than his knowledge of it. Modern maps make no such confession. They are seamless, satellite-fed, total. You can zoom into a street corner in a city you will never visit and read the names of its coffee shops. The feeling this produces is that the world is finished, that exploration is a hobby for historians. But this is an illusion, and the easiest way to see through it is to go down.

[~105]

The ocean covers about seventy percent of the planet, and we have mapped most of it the way you might map a house by flying over it in a plane. We know the broad shape. We do not know the details. By some measures we have better topographic data for Mars than for our own seafloor, because Mars has no water in the way. Roughly a quarter of the ocean bottom has been mapped at high resolution. The rest is a suggestion. And the deep ocean is not merely unmapped but mostly unvisited. More people have stood on the Moon than have stood at the bottom of the Mariana Trench, which is only eleven kilometers down, a distance you could drive in seven minutes on a highway, except that no highway and no sunlight and almost nothing human has ever gone there.

[~135]

Consider the eel. For most of recorded history, nobody could find eel eggs, eel young, or eel reproductive organs, anywhere. Aristotle concluded they emerged spontaneously from mud. Pliny thought they rubbed against rocks and the scrapings came alive. As a young man in Trieste, Sigmund Freud spent a summer dissecting hundreds of eels in search of testes and failed, which is one of the great footnotes in the history of science. It turned out that European eels mature sexually only during a vast migration across the Atlantic to the Sargasso Sea, a fact hypothesized by the Danish oceanographer Johannes Schmidt after two decades of chasing ever-smaller larvae, and only confirmed by tracking tagged adults within the last few years. We have sequenced genomes and landed robots on comets, and until recently we could not tell you where one of the world's common fish goes to reproduce.

[~150]

I love the eel story because it corrects a certain chronological arrogance. We assume the blank spaces on the map were all filled in by our grandparents, that the remaining mysteries live only at the exotic frontiers: dark matter, the origin of life, the first fraction of a second after the Big Bang. But the unknown is not exotic. It is local, patient, and often wet. Nobody knows, in a settled, unified way, why we sleep. We have good theories; memory consolidation, cellular cleanup, the nightly pruning of synapses, and we have the brute fact that every animal with a brain does it at the cost of being defenseless for hours, which means evolution insists on it and we still can't fully say why. You will spend a third of your life doing something science cannot entirely explain. The dragons are in the bedroom.

[~140]

And then there is the most familiar blank space of all: other people. I have never once experienced your experience. I infer it, model it, guess at it from your face and your words, and the guessing works well enough that we build whole civilizations on it, but it remains guessing. Every person you pass on the street is an unmapped interior continent. Even the people you love best are partly legend, partly report, partly your own cartography projected onto them. This sounds lonely, and sometimes it is, but I think it is also the source of everything decent in us. Curiosity about another mind is just respect wearing its work clothes. Love, at least one kind of love, is the decision to keep exploring a coast you will never finish charting.

[~135]

There is an old saying that as the island of knowledge grows, so does the shoreline of wonder. I used to find this discouraging. If every answer births two new questions, then inquiry is a treadmill, and ignorance is infinite either way. But I have come to think the metaphor is actually the best news available. A finite island in an infinite sea means there is no finish line at which curiosity becomes obsolete, no moment when the species closes its notebooks and says done. The map will always have edges, because having edges is what a map is. Total knowledge would not be a completed map. It would be the end of mapmaking, which is to say the end of everything interesting.

[~135]

So I have made my peace with the blank spaces, and more than peace: I have started to think of them as the point. The cartographers of six centuries ago wrote their fear into the margins in the form of dragons, and fear was the wrong emotion, but the impulse was right. Something is out there past the edge of what we know. It has always been out there. The correct caption for the blank was never a warning. It was an invitation.

[~105]
